St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 12 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Message from the Vicar

Rev. Fr. Eby Paulose

Vicar & President
St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church, Bensalem

“Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain.” – Psalm 127:1 Dearly Beloved in Christ, With hearts filled with gratitude to Almighty God, we joyfully celebrate fifty blessed years of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church, Bensalem. This Golden Jubilee is not merely a celebration of five decades, but a testimony to God's unfailing grace, the prayers of generations, the sacrifices of our forefathers, and the enduring faith of a community that has remained steadfast in Christ. As we look back upon this remarkable journey, we remember with profound gratitude our founding Vicar, Very Rev. K. Mathai Cor Episcopos, whose vision, dedication, and leadership laid the spiritual foundations of this parish. We honor all the clergy, office bearers, founding members, and faithful families who labored with love and sacrifice to establish and nurture this spiritual home. Though many of those pioneers are no longer physically among us, their prayers, faith, and legacy continue to bear fruit. This Jubilee also marks a significant moment in our parish's history as we celebrate the election of our beloved Shibu Achan to the Episcopate. His journey from serving this parish to being called to shepherd the wider Church is a source of great joy and thanksgiving. It reminds us that the true fruit of a parish is not measured merely by what it builds, but by the servants of God it nurtures and offers to His Church. May the Lord grant him wisdom, humility, and strength for this sacred ministry. For me, this parish holds a place in my heart that words can hardly express. St. Gregorios Church is not simply the church where I serve as Vicar today; it is the church where my own spiritual and priestly journey unfolded. I had the blessing of serving this altar as a Subdeacon and Deacon, and it was within these sacred walls that I received the Holy Ordination to the priesthood. Here, I began my journey as a priest, and here, I had the joy of celebrating the Holy Baptism of our three children. Some of the most sacred and unforgettable moments of my life and family are deeply rooted in this parish. Therefore, serving this community as its Vicar during this Golden Jubilee year is not merely an assignment; it is a homecoming filled with gratitude, memories, and God's providence. I thank God for bringing my journey back to this spiritual home. As we celebrate fifty years, let us also look toward the next fifty with renewed faith and commitment. The Church is not merely a building or an institution; it is the living Body of Christ, where we encounter Him through the Holy Mysteries, grow in holiness, find healing, and learn to love one another. Our greatest achievement must not simply be what we have built, but the faith we preserve, the unity we nurture, and the Christian life we pass on to our children and future generations. Let our homes become little churches, our families become witnesses of faith, and our parish become a place where everyone experiences the welcoming love of Christ. Let us remember the past with gratitude, live the present with faith, and embrace the future with hope. May the intercession of our heavenly patron, St. Gregorios of Parumala, guide us in humility, prayer, and sacrificial love. May this parish continue to shine as a beacon of Orthodox faith and a spiritual home for generations to come. I sincerely thank our Jubilee Committee, parish leadership, families, volunteers, benefactors, and every member who has contributed to this blessed celebration. Above all, let us give glory to God, who has faithfully guided this parish through fifty years. Fifty years of God's grace behind us, a living faith among us, and a blessed future before us.

With prayers, love, and blessings,
Rev. Fr. Eby Paulose
Vicar & President, St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church, Bensalem

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 13 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Message from the Trustee

From the Trustee’s Desk

Photo

Mr. Thomas Ninan

Trustee
St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church, Bensalem

A church looks one way from the pew and another way from the ledger. From the pew, you see the altar, the candles, and the faces you have known for years. From the ledger, you see the columns. Twenty dollars, fifty, a little more at Christmas, a little less in January, which is how it always goes. And then there is the name that appears every month for eleven years until, one spring, the donation stops. Behind every one of those names was a person who gave what they could, often more than they could. Some moved away. Many have gone home to the Lord. The ledger has not forgotten them, and neither should we. To read the ledger properly, you have to remember where it begins. This Church began in 1976 with no building, no bank account, and no committees. Everything it owned fit into two suitcases, carried in and out every Sunday by our founder, Very Rev. K. Mathai Cor Episcopos, and by a handful of families who came early to set up and stayed behind to pack it all away again. Two suitcases, a few families, and a faith far larger than anything they owned. Those early years were hard. Money was often short, and there were disagreements serious enough to have ended the Church. Instead, those families prayed, forgave one another, and stayed together. Everything that followed was built on that choice.

Slowly, the handful grew, until other parishes in the Diocese began to look to us as an example. No one would call us perfect, but we learned how to endure. We were further shaped by Rev. Fr. Shibu Mathai, now bishop-elect. Achen brought us clarity, discipline, and renewed energy, teaching us to organize, plan, and build with purpose. I did not learn this history from a book; I grew up watching it happen. My father, K. T. Ninan, was the first Trustee of this Church, and I watched him record those early offerings by hand, long before computers or budgets, long before anyone imagined what this place would become. He was not trying to write history. He was simply being faithful with what had been entrusted to him. From a child running through the basement hall to the Trustee writing these words, I have seen nearly every season of this Church’s life. Some of the hands that once carried those suitcases are no longer with us. I carry their memory, as I know many of you do. As we celebrate this Golden Jubilee, I keep returning to four words: My Church, My Responsibility. Words like these are easy to print and easy to forget by February. But fifty years of records tell a simple story. This Church was built by people who took responsibility for it, quietly, faithfully, and at real cost to themselves. To the Clergy who have served us, to the Trustees who kept the accounts honest and the doors open, and to the Secretaries whose records and correspondence hold us together: Thank You. Most of your work goes unseen, but it matters. To every member who has given financially, and to everyone who has volunteered time and labor without expecting recognition: you may have assumed no one noticed. Someone did. Someone wrote it down. Your faithfulness is part of the record, and part of what carried this Church from two suitcases to the beautiful sanctuary we celebrate today. From the pew, you see beauty. From the ledger, you see faithfulness. Fifty years of grace. Fifty years of struggle. Fifty years of forgiveness. Fifty years of generosity. And above all, fifty years of God shaping a Church that is not perfect, but has stayed faithful.

Two suitcases. Fifty years. The story continues, and the next chapter is ours to write.
My Church. My Responsibility.

Thomas Ninan
Trustee

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 14 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Message from the Secretary

Mr. Mathew Madathil Kurian

Parish Secretary
St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church, Bensalem

A Legacy of Faith, A Home for Generations
Celebrating 50 Years of Faith, Family, and Fellowship
“One generation shall praise Your works to another, and shall declare Your mighty acts.” — Psalm 145:4

There are places we visit, places we remember, and places that become a part of who we are. For me, St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church has always been more than a place of worship. It has been my spiritual home, a foundation of my faith, and a constant presence throughout my life. As we celebrate the Golden Jubilee of our beloved parish, I reflect with immense gratitude on the blessing of being part of its remarkable journey. I was once a young child growing up within this church, surrounded by the prayers, traditions, friendships, and love of our parish family. Today, that same church is nurturing my own children. To worship alongside my parents, my wife, and my children, with three generations sharing the same faith and fellowship, is a blessing beyond words. My sincere hope is that decades from now, my children will look back on their childhood in this parish with the same affection and gratitude I carry today. May they remember the friendships, the celebrations, the lessons of faith, and the people who made this church feel like home. Above all, may they recognize that they belong to something far greater than themselves, a living legacy built upon the prayers, sacrifices, and devotion of generations before them. Our fifty-year journey is a testament to what faith, unity, and selfless service can accomplish. From the vision of our founding members to the dedication of those who serve today, each generation has helped shape the parish we proudly call home.

We owe a profound debt of gratitude to our founding Vicar, Very Rev. K. Mathai Cor Episcopos, whose spiritual vision and unwavering dedication laid the foundation for our parish. We are equally grateful for the devoted leadership of our former Vicar and Metropolitan-designate, Very Rev. Geevarghese Ramban (Rev. Fr. Shibu Venad Mathai), whose years of pastoral care have left a lasting imprint on our community. As we enter this new chapter, we warmly embrace our current Vicar, Rev. Fr. Eby Paulose, and look forward with faith and hope to the journey ahead. Their spiritual leadership, together with the contributions of all clergy who have served our parish, remains an enduring blessing. Through God’s abundant grace, St. Gregorios has become a model parish within our diocese and a beacon of hope in the wider community. Our greatest strength lies in our generous, hardworking parish families and our shared desire to live our faith through compassion, service, and love. We strive not only to be faithful members of our Church, but also responsible citizens and a meaningful presence in the world around us. Serving as Parish Secretary during this historic Golden Jubilee has been one of the greatest honors and blessings of my life. To serve the very parish that helped raise me, at such a momentous occasion in its history, is a privilege I will cherish forever. This experience has deepened my appreciation for the countless individuals whose quiet sacrifices and tireless efforts sustain our parish. As we celebrate fifty years, let us remember that our Golden Jubilee is not simply a celebration of our past, but a responsibility to our future. The greatest tribute we can offer those who came before us is to ensure that the faith, unity, and love they cultivated continue to flourish for generations to come. To our founding families, spiritual fathers, past and present leaders, volunteers, and every parish member who has contributed to this extraordinary journey, I extend my heartfelt gratitude. May our parish continue to be a place where faith is nurtured, families are strengthened, and generations find a spiritual home.

With gratitude, faith, and hope for the generations to come.
Mathew Madathil Kurian
Parish Secretary

With Profound Joy and Gratitude

Rev. Fr. K. P. Varghese

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church, Bensalem

It is with profound joy and gratitude that I write to congratulate St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church of Bensalem, on the joyous occasion of its Golden Jubilee. This house of worship stands as a glorious testament to God's presence and a beautiful expression of His love for the community.

While I was the Vicar of St. Thomas Indian Orthodox Church of Baltimore, I was familiar with this Church. I wish every family the choicest blessings of our Heavenly Father. May the intercession of our patron saint, St. Gregorios of Parumala, remain a fortress of faith for us all.

Rev. Fr. K. P. Varghese

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 21 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Rev. Fr. Alexander Kurien

The Promises No One Speaks

What the Faithful Quietly Expect of Their Shepherds

Rev. Fr. Alexander James Kurien

Senior Orthodox Priest
Senior Executive, United States Government, Washington, DC

In thirty-nine years of priesthood, no parishioner has ever sat across from me and listed what they expect of me. No one hands a new priest a contract. No one reads the terms aloud at his ordination. Yet the terms are there. They are written in the eyes of the widow who waits by the door after the Holy Qurbana, in the silence of the young man who lingers in the last pew, in the voice of the mother who calls late at night and apologizes for calling at all. The faithful carry expectations of their spiritual leaders that they rarely voice but always feel, and by those expectations they quietly and honestly measure whether the shepherd can be trusted.

I have come to believe that most departures from a church, most cooling of faith, and most slow drifting away begin not with a quarrel over doctrine but with one of these unspoken promises being broken. Not shouted about. Noted and remembered. So let me try to say aloud what the faithful so seldom say.

The First Expectation: That You Will Be There

Our Lord called Himself the Good Shepherd who knows His sheep by name and whose sheep know His voice (John 10:14). Notice the order. Knowing comes before leading. The faithful do not first ask whether their priest is eloquent, learned, or gifted in administration. They ask, without words, “Will he come when I need him?”

Every priest knows the call that comes from a hospital corridor. Every priest knows the funeral that disrupts a carefully planned week. In those hours, a sermon is not required. Presence is. I have learned that people forget most of what I preach, but they never forget who stood beside the bed when their father drew his last breath. The ministry of presence is not a small part of the priesthood. It may well be the largest. When a shepherd is too busy to come, the flock rarely complains. They conclude they were never truly known, and people do not stay long where they are not known.

The Second Expectation: That You Will Live What You Preach

St. Peter, writing to the elders of the early Church, urged them to shepherd the flock not as lords over those in their charge but as examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:3). St. Paul told young Timothy to be an example to the believers in word, conduct, love, spirit, faith, and purity (1 Timothy 4:12).

The faithful listen to our homilies, but they watch our lives. They notice how we speak to the altar server who made a mistake. They notice whether we are generous or grasping, whether we hold grudges or forgive, and whether we kneel in prayer when no one is watching. A child in the third row may not remember the theology of the Incarnation, but he will remember whether his priest was kind.

St. John Chrysostom, who wrote so beautifully about the dignity of the priesthood, warned that a priest’s faults cannot remain hidden because he stands on a height where every soul can see him. It is a frightening and holy truth. Our integrity is never a private matter. It is the soil in which the faith of others either grows or withers.

The Third Expectation: That You Will Point Beyond Yourself

This one is subtle and perhaps the most dangerous to neglect. The faithful, often without realizing it, hope that their shepherd will lead them somewhere they could never reach alone. Not to a larger building or a busier calendar, but closer to God.

St. John the Baptist understood this perfectly. When his own disciples began following Jesus, he did not grieve. He said, “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). A true shepherd measures success not by how many people admire him, but by how many he has handed over to Christ.

There is a quiet temptation in every ministry to become the center: to be needed, to be praised, to gather a following more attached to the priest than to the Lord. When that happens, the day the priest is transferred, falls ill, or disappoints, the people’s faith collapses with him. But when a shepherd has always pointed beyond himself, the flock remains standing because they were never leaning on him in the first place.

The Fourth Expectation: That You Will Tell the Truth in Love

People do not want a shepherd who only comforts, nor one who only corrects. They want one who speaks the truth in love (Ephesians 4:15). They want the hard thing said gently and the gentle thing said honestly. A priest who flatters is soon distrusted. A priest who wounds is soon avoided. Between the two lies the narrow road of the true pastor, and it is walked only with much prayer.

When the Shepherd Fails

I would be dishonest if I pretended that any of us kept these promises perfectly. I certainly have not. There were calls I returned too late, words I spoke too sharply, and seasons when I was more tired than faithful.

Here, the Gospel holds out great mercy. Peter denied his Lord three times. Yet on the shore of Galilee, the risen Christ asked him three times, “Do you love Me?” and gave him the same charge three times: “Feed My sheep” (John 21:15–17). The commission was not withdrawn because of failure. It was renewed through repentance and love. That is the hope of every honest shepherd.

The Shepherd Is Also a Sheep

Perhaps the deepest truth I have learned over nearly four decades at the holy altar is this: I can keep none of these promises by my own strength. I cannot be everywhere. I cannot lead anyone to God unless He first leads me. The priest is a shepherd, yes, but he is also a sheep in the flock of the one Chief Shepherd (1 Peter 5:4). We can give only what we ourselves receive in prayer, in repentance, in the Holy Mysteries, and at the feet of Christ.

I offer a simple practice to my brother priests and to all who lead in the Church. Now and then, sit quietly with the names of those entrusted to you and ask three honest questions. Have they seen me present? Have they seen Christ in how I live? Am I leading them toward Him or toward me?

We will not always like the answers, but asking is itself an act of faithfulness. And the Lord, who called us knowing each of our weaknesses, will supply all that we lack.

Rev. Fr. Alexander James Kurien

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 22 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Mrs. Ceena Mathew • Associate Minister

Jubilee: A Sacred Journey of God’s Faithfulness

Mrs. Ceena Mathew

Associate Minister
St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church

There are moments in the life of a church when we are invited to pause—not merely to count the years, but to remember the prayers that sustained us, the hands that labored, and the generations that carried the faith forward. A Jubilee is such a moment.

In Leviticus 25, God established the Jubilee as a sacred time of restoration, freedom, and new beginnings. At its heart was this profound reminder: “The land is Mine; for you are strangers and sojourners with Me” (Leviticus 25:23). Jubilee reminds us that everything we possess is entrusted to us by God, and every blessing ultimately comes from Him. The biblical Jubilee was more than a festival. It was a declaration of God's sovereignty, a restoration of relationships, and a reminder that His people were called to live with justice, compassion, and trust in Him.

As we celebrate our parish Jubilee, we look back with grateful hearts upon a journey marked by God’s abundant grace. God has incredibly blessed our parish. Through the faith, prayers, sacrifices, and dedication of generations, He has nurtured our community in ways our founders may never have imagined. We give thanks for our clergy, families, faithful servants, children, and all who have contributed to the life of our parish. Those who planted the seeds of faith before us may no longer be physically present, but their legacy continues to bear fruit.

At the heart of our Malankara Orthodox tradition is a living faith centered on Jesus Christ and nourished through the Holy Qurbana, prayer, Scripture, and the sacramental life of the Church. We have received a precious inheritance, one that we are called not merely to preserve, but to live faithfully and pass on to future generations.

Jubilee is more than a remembrance of the past; it is an invitation to renewal. Just as the biblical Jubilee called people to restoration and a fresh beginning, may this celebration renew our commitment to Christ, strengthen our fellowship, heal divisions, and inspire us to serve one another and the wider community with love. We must also ask ourselves: What will the next generation inherit from us? Beyond buildings, programs, and accomplishments, may they inherit a vibrant faith, a spirit of prayer, a heart for service, and a deep love for the Holy Church.

As we celebrate this milestone, let us look back with gratitude, live in the present with faith, and look toward the future with hope. The God who has faithfully guided and richly blessed our parish will continue to lead us in the years ahead.

The years are our history. Faith is our inheritance. The future is our responsibility. And every blessing is a testimony to the faithfulness of God.

To God alone be the glory.

Ceena Mathew

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 23 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

From Shepherd to Metropolitan

Very Rev. Geevarghese Ramban • Rev. Fr. Shibu Venad Mathai

A Journey of Faith, Service, and Grace

“I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will feed you with knowledge and understanding.” — Jeremiah 3:15

There are individuals whose presence leaves an impression, and there are those whose lives leave a legacy. In the history of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church, Bensalem, Pennsylvania, Rev. Fr. Shibu Venad Mathai, affectionately known to generations of faithful as Shibu Achen, holds a special place. His journey is one of unwavering faith, humble beginnings, devoted priestly service, and an extraordinary calling that has now led him toward the episcopacy of the Holy Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church.

As our parish celebrates its Golden Jubilee, marking fifty years of faith, fellowship, and spiritual growth, we reflect with gratitude on the remarkable contributions of a shepherd who dedicated a significant chapter of his priestly life to our church and its people.

A Journey Rooted in Faith

The spiritual journey of Shibu Achen began in India, where his roots were firmly established in the Orthodox Christian faith. His home parish, St. Mary’s Orthodox Church in Thaloor, The Nilgiris, within the Sulthan Bathery Diocese, provided the foundation for a life that would eventually extend far beyond the borders of his homeland.

His educational journey reflects a commitment to both intellectual development and spiritual formation. After earning a Bachelor of Science degree in Physics from Calicut University, he pursued theological studies, completing his Bachelor of Divinity at Orthodox Theological Seminary between 1997 and 2001, followed by a Master of Theology at FFRRC from 2003 to 2005.

These years of preparation helped shape not only his understanding of Orthodox theology and tradition but also his approach to pastoral ministry — one grounded in faith, strengthened by knowledge, and guided by compassion.

In 2005, he was ordained to the holy priesthood by His Grace Kuriyakose Mar Clemis, beginning what would become more than two decades of dedicated service to Christ and His Church.

A Calling That Crossed Continents

Shibu Achen began his priestly ministry as Assistant Vicar at St. Mary’s Orthodox Cathedral Pilgrim Center in Sulthan Bathery, serving from 2005 to 2008. These formative years provided invaluable pastoral experience and strengthened his commitment to serving the faithful.

In 2008, his ministry brought him to the United States, where he served as Assistant Vicar of St. Gregorios Orthodox Church in Oak Park (Elmhurst), Illinois, until 2011.

Serving the Orthodox faithful in America presented a unique calling. Here, the Church was not only a place of worship but also a spiritual home for families navigating life between two cultures. Preserving the richness of Orthodox faith and tradition while helping younger generations find their own spiritual identity became an essential part of pastoral ministry.

It was a responsibility that would become central to the next and perhaps most defining chapter of his priestly journey.

A Shepherd Who Became Part of Our Parish Family

In 2011, Shibu Achen began his ministry as Vicar of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church in Bensalem, Pennsylvania. What followed was fifteen years of pastoral service that would leave a lasting imprint on the spiritual life of our parish.

Over those years, he became much more than the priest who celebrated the Holy Qurbana on Sundays. He became a spiritual guide, teacher, counselor, mentor, and a familiar presence through the many seasons of parish life.

For countless families, Shibu Achen was present during life’s most meaningful moments — celebrating marriages, welcoming children into the Church through Holy Baptism, encouraging young people as they grew in faith, comforting families during times of illness, and offering prayers and strength during moments of loss.

His ministry extended beyond the sanctuary. Through parish gatherings, Sunday School, youth activities, spiritual discussions, and personal interactions, he helped strengthen the bonds that make a parish more than a congregation — a true family united in Christ.

Perhaps one of the most meaningful aspects of his legacy is the influence he has had across generations.

Children who once attended Sunday School under his pastoral guidance have grown into young adults. Young people have pursued higher education, established careers, and begun families of their own. Parents and grandparents have witnessed the continued growth of the Church while remaining connected to the traditions and values they brought from their homeland.

Through these changing seasons, Shibu Achen remained a spiritual presence, reminding us that while the world around us may change, our foundation in Christ must remain steadfast.

His years in Bensalem demonstrate a profound truth about pastoral leadership: the measure of a shepherd is not merely the number of years he serves, but the faith he inspires, the relationships he builds, and the spiritual foundation he leaves for future generations.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 24 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

From Shepherd to Metropolitan

Very Rev. Geevarghese Ramban • Rev. Fr. Shibu Venad Mathai

A Ministry Beyond Parish Boundaries

While his service to St. Gregorios remained a defining part of his priestly journey, Shibu Achen’s contributions extended throughout the Northeast American Diocese and the wider Christian community.

He served as a Diocesan Council member, Director of the Holy Transfiguration Retreat Center in Dalton, Pennsylvania, and faculty member for Divyabodhanam and diocesan leadership training programs.

His commitment to young people and Christian leadership was also reflected in his previous responsibilities as Secretary of OCYM in the Sulthan Bathery Diocese, Regional Secretary of the OCYM Northern Region, Vice President of MGOCSM in the Northeast American Diocese, and Spiritual Advisor to Youth Ministry in Philadelphia.

His involvement in the wider Christian community included serving as Chairman and Co-Chairman of the Ecumenical Fellowship of Indian Churches in Pennsylvania in 2017 and 2024.

Beyond formal leadership positions, his ministry has embraced the Christian responsibility of caring for those in need. Through parish mission initiatives and personal outreach, he has supported underprivileged families through educational assistance, career guidance, financial aid, and charitable partnerships.

These efforts reflect a conviction that Christian ministry cannot be confined to the walls of a church. True discipleship is expressed through compassion, service, and a willingness to recognize Christ in those who need our help.

From Faithful Priest to a Higher Calling

The year 2026 marked an extraordinary milestone in Shibu Achen’s spiritual journey.

On August 27, 2026, he was selected as Metropolitan-designate, a historic moment that recognized more than two decades of priestly ministry and entrusted him with the sacred responsibility of preparing for episcopal leadership.

For those who had known him throughout his years of service, this was a moment of immense joy, gratitude, and spiritual significance.

On October 27, 2026, he received the monastic tonsure and became Very Rev. Geevarghese Ramban, marking another important step in his preparation for the episcopacy.

His Episcopal Consecration is scheduled for February 4, 2027, when, God willing, he will enter a new chapter of service as a bishop of the Holy Church.

For our parish, these milestones carry a deeply personal meaning. The priest who had walked alongside our families, guided our children, prayed at our altars, and shared in our joys and sorrows was now being called to shepherd the faithful in a greater capacity.

Yet the beauty of this journey lies in its continuity. The same spirit of service that characterized his priestly ministry remains the foundation of his higher calling.

A bishop’s calling is not a departure from the heart of a priest, but an expansion of the responsibility to love, guide, protect, and serve God’s people.

A Legacy That Will Live Through Generations

As St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church celebrates fifty years of its spiritual journey, we are reminded that the history of a parish is written not only through buildings, milestones, and celebrations, but through the people who have faithfully nurtured its growth.

Shibu Achen’s fifteen years of service form an important chapter of that history.

His legacy lives in the prayers offered at our altar, in the children who learned to love their Orthodox faith, in the young adults who found encouragement and direction, in the families who experienced comfort during difficult times, and in the countless relationships strengthened through fellowship and service.

The true impact of a spiritual father is often revealed not in a single moment, but over a lifetime. A word of encouragement offered to a child may shape a future leader. A prayer shared with a struggling family may restore hope. A lesson taught in faith may remain in someone’s heart for decades.

These are the quiet yet powerful ways in which a priest influences generations.

As he prepares to embrace the sacred responsibilities of episcopal ministry, we celebrate not only his accomplishments but also the example his journey offers to every member of our community.

His life reminds us that faithfulness in small responsibilities prepares us for greater ones, that genuine leadership begins with service, and that God’s calling often unfolds in ways beyond our imagination.

From the hills of The Nilgiris to the churches of America, from the ministry of a parish priest to the calling of a Metropolitan, his journey stands as a testimony to the grace of God working through a life dedicated to His service.

For the faithful of St. Gregorios, Bensalem, he will always remain our beloved Shibu Achen — a shepherd who became part of our families, a teacher who helped shape our faith, and a spiritual father whose influence will continue to be felt for generations.

As we honor fifty golden years of our parish, we offer our heartfelt gratitude for his ministry and our prayers for the sacred journey ahead.

May the Lord who called him to serve continue to strengthen, guide, and bless him as he prepares to shepherd His flock in this new chapter of ministry.

His journey is a reminder that the greatest legacy we can leave behind is not what we accomplish for ourselves, but what we inspire in others through faith, love, and service.

— Lyn Kurien

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 27 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

History

Nasrani History

From St. Thomas to Syrians

By Neil Mathew

When most people think of India and religion, they immediately think of Hinduism, or maybe to a lesser extent Sikhism or Islam. Very few people would even consider Christianity, and if they do, they assume it is a holdover of European colonialism. However, this couldn’t be farther from the truth; Christianity is one of India's oldest continuous religions, dating back to the Apostolic Age. It in fact predated European Christianity, existing centuries before Constantine’s conversion. As such, it is important to examine the inception and growth of Christianity in India, and how it led to the current state of the Malankara Orthodox faith.

St. Thomas in India

Tradition holds that Christianity first reached India in 52 A.D. by St. Thomas the Apostle, who landed in Cranganore. It was here that he first started preaching primarily to Brahmins and Jews (many trader and merchant settlements were established by Jews), and established 7 churches, known as the Ezharappallikal. This is further corroborated by the Church Fathers, particularly St. Eusebius of Caesarea, who stated that when St. Pantaenus, a prominent Alexandrian theologian, arrived in Kerala in 190 A.D., he found the Christians using a version of the Gospel of Matthew that included both Hebrew and Syriac wording. The inclusion of Syriac wording is particularly interesting, as it is a dialect of Aramaic, the language Jesus and his Disciples would have spoken.

Growth under Church of the East

Over the next few centuries, the Church in Kerala benefited from the large-scale trade between the Malabar Coast and the Middle East, as many Syrian Christian traders would end up settling in the region. Over time, particularly during the Medieval period, the Church in Kerala coalesced under the Church of the East, a Persian Nestorian Church, who would provide structure and theological guidance. In this system, the Church in Kerala benefited from autonomy and self-governance, but derived its theology and liturgy from the Church of the East. Additionally, the Christian community was well-integrated into the social fabric of Kerala, and even highly esteemed; copper plates dated between the eighth and

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 28 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

History

thirteenth centuries indicated that the Christians were granted special rights, particularly exemptions from certain taxes and import duties, which were typically reserved for important dignitaries.

The Portuguese Catholics and Syrian Orthodox

This flourishing of the Indian Christian community continued until the sixteenth century, when Portuguese Catholic presence increased in the region coupled with diminishing influence of the Church of the East. The Portuguese Catholics were fiercely opposed to the practices descended from the Church of the East, partly due to the Nestorian nature, and also to the lack of allegiance to the Roman Pope. These tensions culminated in the Synod of Diamper, which forcibly brought the Malayalee Christians of the Archdiocese of Angamaly under the Latin Archdiocese of Goa. This led to the latinization of Malayalee Christian practices, which had been preserved for multiple centuries. Additionally, the autonomy the community had enjoyed for over a millenia was being infringed upon, as matters of governance were required to be submitted to foreign authorities. In opposition to this, many clergy and laity took part in the Coonan Cross Oath, by which they pledged on a cross that they would resist latinization and return to ancient practices. In doing so, they were assisted by Syriac Orthodox Church, who sent Bishops to strengthen the community, leading to the start of Orthodox Christianity in Kerala.

Present Day

Despite the tumultuous struggle Christians have faced in India, it is by the Holy Spirit that the community was able to continue, eventually culminating in the adoption of the Orthodox faith. This adoption brought the Church in line with other Ancient Christian faiths located around the world, such as the Coptic and Armenian Orthodox Churches. However, despite this adoption of faith and theology, the traditions of the Church have remained steadfast over time, preserving identity and heritage, thus making Christianity inherently native to India.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 29 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

A Pilgrimage of Faith

The Fifty-Year Journey of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church, 1976–2026

By Manoj Chacko, Reji Ninan and Shiju Poovathoor

The Seeds of Faith

Early Malayalee Christian Fellowship in Philadelphia

The 1960s saw the arrival of a growing number of Christians from Kerala, India, to the Philadelphia area for higher education, employment, and other professional opportunities. They represented several Christian traditions, including the Orthodox, Jacobite, Catholic, Mar Thoma, CSI, and Knanaya Churches. Although they came from different denominations, they shared a common language, culture, and faith in Jesus Christ. At the time, none of these communities had a large enough presence in Philadelphia to maintain its own parish and resident priest. As a result, Malayalee Christians came together as an ecumenical fellowship, gathering in one another’s homes for prayer and fellowship and welcoming visiting priests and bishops to conduct worship services.

A significant milestone came in July 1962, when the first recorded Malayalam liturgical service for the Malayalee Christian community in Philadelphia was celebrated in the living room of Late Dr. T. V. Philip, one of the pioneer members of our church, at his apartment at 4900 Pine Street, Philadelphia. Rev. Fr. K. M. Simon of the Knanaya Church was the celebrant. The historical record notes that Dr. Philip himself served as the acolyte for that first service. Beginning in August 1962, regular services were held on the first Sunday of each month at the chapel of Asbury Methodist Church on Chestnut Street.

Late Rev. Fr. Dr. Paul Varki, who was a deacon during those early years and had come to the United States for higher studies, later became a coordinator of the ecumenical congregation. He helped arrange services by contacting available priests in Philadelphia and neighboring areas and inviting them to celebrate the Holy Qurbana and lead the faithful in worship. As the number of faithful increased, the congregation eventually moved from the chapel at Asbury Methodist Church to the chapel of the Episcopal Church of the Savior at 38th and Chestnut Streets in Philadelphia.

This fellowship had no formal denominational affiliation and was not an incorporated parish. It was, rather, a community of Malayalee Christians brought together by a shared desire to worship and remain rooted in their faith while building new lives far from their homeland. These humble gatherings planted the seeds from which an organized Orthodox Christian community in Philadelphia would soon emerge.

From Fellowship to Parish

The Birth of the First Orthodox Parish in Philadelphia - 1976

The ecumenical fellowship of the 1960s and early 1970s had nurtured the faith of Malayalee Christians in Philadelphia, but for the Orthodox faithful, the desire for a parish of their own continued to grow. Until 1976, there was no officially established Malankara Orthodox parish or resident Orthodox priest in Philadelphia. The American Diocese itself had not yet been formed; Orthodox parishes in the United States and Canada were then under the jurisdiction of the Bombay Diocese.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 30 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

A decisive moment came during Holy Week in April 1976. At the invitation of then Dn. Dr. Paul Varki, Late Very Rev. K. Mathai Cor Episcopos came from New York to serve as the chief celebrant for the Holy Week services of the ecumenical congregation, beginning with the Pesaha Thursday evening service and continuing through Easter Sunday. Approximately sixty Orthodox faithful from the Philadelphia area participated. The presence and pastoral leadership of Mathai Achen made a deep impression on the community and strengthened a growing hope: that Philadelphia might finally have an Orthodox parish of its own, with Mathai Achen as its priest.

That hope could not be realized immediately. Mathai Achen was living and working in New York, and family and professional responsibilities made relocation difficult. Yet the Orthodox faithful in Philadelphia continued to encourage him to move and help establish a parish. In September 1976, after prayerful consideration, Mathai Achen and his family moved permanently to Philadelphia. What had long been a hope was now beginning to take shape.

On October 10, 1976, Mathai Achen convened a general meeting of Orthodox faithful living in Philadelphia. The purpose of the gathering was to consider formally the establishment of an Orthodox parish in Philadelphia. After discussion, the members unanimously adopted two historic resolutions: to organize an Orthodox parish in the City of Brotherly Love under the Malankara Orthodox Church in India, and to name the newly formed parish as St. Thomas Orthodox Church of India at Philadelphia. Mathai Achen became the first Vicar of this newly established parish.

The resolutions were forwarded to His Holiness Baselios Marthoma Mathews I, Catholicos of the East and to H.G. Dr. Thomas Mar Makarios, then Metropolitan of the Bombay Diocese. Because the American Diocese would not be established until 1979, the Orthodox churches and congregations in the United States and Canada were at that time under the Bombay Diocese. A Kalpana was subsequently issued in 1976 recognizing St. Thomas Orthodox Church of India at Philadelphia as a parish of the Malankara Orthodox Church. Thus, the first officially recognized Malankara Orthodox parish in Philadelphia was born.

Around January 24th 1980, the parish was incorporated with the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania as a religious nonprofit organization. Regular Sunday worship was conducted by Mathai Achen at the chapel of the Church of the Savior at 38th and Chestnut Streets in Philadelphia. H.G. Dr. Thomas Mar Makarios later visited and blessed the parish. With membership of more than sixty families, the young parish entered a new period of organized worship, ministry, and growth.

The journey that had begun with small ecumenical gatherings in homes and rented chapels had now reached a defining milestone. Philadelphia's Orthodox faithful now had an officially recognized parish, a Vicar, and a spiritual home of their own. Yet this was only the beginning. The years ahead would bring remarkable growth, new ministries, difficult transitions, and ultimately the emergence of the parish we know today as St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 31 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

Through Trial to Renewal

The Reorganization and Formation of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church (1984–1988)

The establishment of St. Thomas Malankara Orthodox Church in 1976 marked an important chapter in the life of Orthodox Christians in Philadelphia. Under the spiritual leadership of Rev. Fr. K. Mathai (Mathai Achen), the parish grew and its ministries developed. However, the early years were not without challenges. Differences arose among members concerning the leadership and future direction of the parish, and over time these disagreements became increasingly difficult to resolve within the congregation.

Seeking a resolution to the growing differences, the matter was brought before the Diocesan Metropolitan, H.G. Dr. Thomas Mar Makarios. On July 1, 1984, Makarios Thirumeni convened a General Body meeting at the Church of the Savior Cathedral in Philadelphia. At this meeting, the General Body adopted a resolution calling for the dissolution of St. Thomas Orthodox Church of India at Philadelphia, Inc., and requested the Metropolitan to establish two separate congregations to accommodate the differing groups within the parish. Mathai Achen, who had faithfully guided the community since its establishment, opposed the division, holding firmly to the hope that the parish could remain united.

Following the General Body's resolution, on November 1, 1984, Makarios Thirumeni issued two Kalpanas (ecclesiastical orders), Nos. 68/84/par and 69/84/par, formally recognizing two parishes within the American Diocese. Kalpana No. 69/84/par established St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church and appointed Rev. Fr. K. Mathai as its Vicar, while Kalpana No. 68/84/par recognized St. Baselios Malankara Orthodox Church. The majority of the members of the former St. Thomas parish, including Dn. Dr. Paul Varki, continued their spiritual journey under Mathai Achen's leadership as members of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church.

The reorganization marked a difficult and painful chapter in the life of the community. The Metropolitan's decisions were subsequently challenged through legal proceedings in the Court of Common Pleas of Delaware County, Pennsylvania (Case No. 85-11387). The dispute raised important questions concerning the authority of the Diocesan Metropolitan, parish governance, and the application of the Constitution of the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church.

During this period, the matter also received the attention of the Holy Episcopal Synod, which met at the Sophia Center Chapel of the Old Seminary in Kottayam from February 23 to 27, 1987. The Holy Synod ratified the actions taken by the Diocesan Metropolitan in organizing the two congregations as St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church and St. Baselios Malankara Orthodox Church. Subsequently, on March 11, 1987, through Kalpana No. 60/87, His Holiness Baselios Mar Thoma Mathews I directed the faithful to abide by the Kalpana of the Diocesan Metropolitan.

A decisive milestone came on December 12, 1988, when the Honorable Judge William R. Toal, Jr., issued a Final Decree ordering the dissolution of St. Thomas Orthodox Church of India in Philadelphia and affirming the formation and incorporation of the two congregations in accordance with the directives of the Holy Episcopal Synod. The Court also directed that the assets and funds of the former parish be distributed between the two congregations. Accordingly, on December 28, 1988, Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, Department of State, dissolved St. Thomas Orthodox Church of India at Philadelphia, Inc. (Corporation No. 701737) The outcome represented a significant victory for the Malankara Orthodox Church in America, affirming the importance of its constitutional framework and the ecclesiastical authority of the Diocesan Metropolitan in matters of parish administration and governance. What began as a painful division thus became a defining moment in the Church's history, establishing the foundation for two distinct parishes to continue their spiritual missions.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 32 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

In Search of a Home

Faith and Perseverance on the Journey - 1984-1995

Despite the challenges surrounding the parish's reorganization, the faithful of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church continued their journey with determination and hope. Although the parish had a new identity and a committed congregation, the dream of having a permanent church home remained unfulfilled. After briefly worshipping at a Presbyterian church in Lansdowne, Pennsylvania, the parish returned to the familiar chapel of the Church of the Savior at 38th and Chestnut Streets in Philadelphia. There, the congregation continued to worship for years, holding firmly to the hope that one day it would have a church of its own.

Life without a permanent home brought many practical challenges. Church supplies and items needed for worship had to be transported from place to place, often carried in suitcases and set up wherever services were held. The lack of dedicated space also made it difficult to conduct Sunday School, ministry programs, meetings, and other spiritual activities. Yet these limitations did not weaken the parish. Through persistence, sacrifice, and faith, the congregation continued to worship, serve, and grow.

As parish membership increased, the need for a permanent home became more urgent. Changes in the management of the Church of the Savior also placed increasing pressure on SGMOC to find another location. The dream of having a church of its own was no longer simply a desire; it had become essential for the continued growth of the parish and its ministries.

In 1994, that dream appeared to be within reach when SGMOC purchased approximately 1.5 acres of land with a house at 9897 Verree Road in Philadelphia. The parish hoped to construct a new church on the property and moved forward with extensive preparations. The Church Building Committee worked diligently on the project, architectural plans were prepared, required approvals and permits were pursued, and a construction company was engaged. In the meantime, Holy Qurbana and other services continued at the property.

After so much preparation and anticipation, however, the parish encountered serious zoning difficulties. The planned construction was halted just as work was expected to begin. Although the parish appealed the decision and continued its efforts to move the project forward, permission to construct the proposed church was ultimately not obtained. It was a painful disappointment after years of prayer, planning, and hard work.

Still, the setback at Verree Road did not end the parish's search. What seemed at the time to be a closed door would soon lead the faithful to another opportunity—one that would finally give St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church a place it could call its own.

A Place to Call Our Own

The Torresdale Avenue Years - 1995-2008

In 1995, soon after the disappointment at Verree Road, SGMOC purchased a small church building and its surrounding property at 7721–31 Torresdale Avenue in Philadelphia. The property had already been used as a religious institution and offered something the parish had sought for nearly two decades: a dedicated place of worship. With the sale of the Verree Road property and the purchase of the Torresdale Avenue church, the dream of having a church of its own had finally become a reality after years of worshipping in borrowed and rented spaces.

The new church was dedicated for Orthodox worship by H.G. Thomas Mar Thimothios, then Catholicos-designate, later became the seventh Catholicos of the East, H.H Moran Mar Baselios Marthoma Didymos I, assisted by H.G. Mathews Mar Barnabas, Metropolitan of the American Diocese, and H.G. Dr. Thomas Mar Makarios, Metropolitan of Canada, USA and Europe. For the members who had carried the parish through years of uncertainty and transition, the dedication marked a joyful and deeply meaningful milestone in their pilgrimage.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 33 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

The Torresdale years became a period of significant spiritual growth and cherished memories. Parish membership increased rapidly, and the church witnessed important occasions in its history, including the elevation of Mathai Achen as Cor Episcopos and the celebration of the 25th anniversary of his priestly ordination. The parish also hosted numerous diocesan and Philadelphia-area programs, including OVBS, MGOCSM activities, and other spiritual and fellowship events.

Although the parish was grateful to finally have a church of its own, the Torresdale facility was small and offered limited space for a rapidly growing congregation. There was no adequate parking area, and the church lacked sufficient rooms for Sunday School, ministry activities, fellowship gatherings, and larger parish events. As membership continued to grow, these limitations became increasingly apparent.

The Torresdale church had fulfilled an important dream: it gave SGMOC its first permanent home. But the very growth made possible during those years created a new challenge. The parish now needed not merely a place to worship, but a larger spiritual home capable of serving its children, families, ministries, and future generations. Once again, the faithful began to look ahead - and the next stage of the pilgrimage would eventually lead them beyond Philadelphia to Bensalem.

A Vision Takes Root

The Journey to Bensalem – 2005–2008

With increasing membership and expanding Sunday School, ministry, and fellowship activities, the General Body recognized the need for a larger property that could serve not only the needs of the present congregation, but also those of future generations. After an extensive search and consideration of several possibilities, the parish's journey led beyond Philadelphia to Bensalem, Pennsylvania.

On June 30, 2005, SGMOC purchased approximately 2.5 acres of land with a house at 4136 Hulmeville Road, Bensalem. The property offered the parish a promising opportunity to build the larger church it had envisioned. However, this land alone was not sufficient to meet the applicable zoning requirements. To make the project possible, the parish acquired the adjoining property at 4150 Hulmeville Road, consisting of approximately 1.75 additional acres, on September 18, 2006. With the combined properties, the vision of a new church campus began to take shape. The Torresdale property was subsequently sold, and the parish moved temporarily to a rented facility in Northeast Philadelphia while preparations for the new church continued.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 34 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

The Bensalem project quickly became a shared undertaking of the entire parish. Members volunteered their time and labor over many weeks to clear and prepare the property. Yet the parish's vision extended beyond constructing a building. Even before moving to Bensalem, SGMOC sought to establish a relationship with its new neighbors. On August, 2007, the church organized its first community event at the property, Community Awareness Day. The event was warmly received, with many neighbors and members of the surrounding community participating. It marked an early expression of the parish's desire to become not simply a church located in Bensalem, but an active part of the Bensalem community.

Another historic milestone came on May 27, 2007, when the parish broke ground for its future church under the leadership of its Vicar, Late Very Rev. K. Mathai Cor Episcopos. For a congregation whose pilgrimage had taken it through homes, borrowed chapels, and rented facilities, the groundbreaking represented far more than the beginning of a construction project. It was the visible beginning of a long-awaited dream.

On March 30, 2008, under the prayerful guidance of Late H.G. Mathews Mar Barnabas, then Metropolitan of the American Diocese, the foundation stone for the new church was laid. Construction moved forward through the dedication of many selfless individuals and the collective prayers, sacrifices, hard work, and generosity of parish families. What had once seemed a distant hope gradually rose from the Bensalem property as a new spiritual home.

By the end of 2008, the long-cherished dream had become a reality. On Christmas Day, December 25, 2008, the parish began worshipping at its new home in Bensalem. The occasion marked the culmination of decades of searching and perseverance—from carrying worship supplies between temporary locations to finally gathering for Holy Qurbana in a church built through the faith and sacrifice of the community.

A Sacred Milestone

Holy Relics and Consecration – 2009

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 35 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

The move to Bensalem marked the beginning of a blessed new chapter for SGMOC. On March 21, 2009, the parish was blessed to receive Holy Relics of its Patron Saint, St. Geevarghese Mar Gregorios of Parumala, the first canonized saint of the Malankara Orthodox Church. The relics were received at Parumala from Late Lamented H.G. Geevarghese Mar Osthathios by our Vicar, Late Very Rev. K. Mathai Cor Episcopos, and a group of parish members. Upon their arrival in the United States, many faithful traveled to JFK Airport in New York to prayerfully receive them. Today, the Holy Relics are reverently enshrined in our church.

Just two months later, another historic milestone followed with the Holy Consecration of the new church on May 22–23, 2009. The consecration services were led by our Diocesan Metropolitan, Late Lamented H.G. Mathews Mar Barnabas, and H.G. Zachariah Mar Nicholovos, with the participation of H.G. Dr. Mathews Mar Severios, the current Catholicos of the East and Malankara Metropolitan, and H.G. Dr. Yuhanon Mar Meletius, along with clergy, dignitaries, and faithful. The consecration prayerfully completed the parish's long journey toward establishing a permanent house of worship and formally dedicated its new spiritual home to the glory of God.

A New Chapter of Leadership

2011

The year 2011 marked an important chapter in the history of SGMOC. On May 21, the parish had the honor of hosting the Sunthroneeso (Enthronement) of H.G. Zachariah Mar Nicholovos as Metropolitan of the Northeast American Diocese. His Holiness Moran Mar Baselios Marthoma Paulos II, Catholicos of the East and Malankara Metropolitan, presided over the Rite of Enthronement, assisted by H.G. Joshua Mar Nicodemus, Metropolitan of the Diocese of Nilackal. With more than one thousand faithful in attendance, the clergy and faithful proclaimed “OXIOS” to their newly enthroned Metropolitan. Hierarchs representing sister dioceses, the Armenian Orthodox Church, and the Episcopal Church also participated in this historic occasion.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 36 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

The year also marked the close of an extraordinary chapter of leadership with the retirement of our founding Vicar, Late Very Rev. K. Mathai Cor Episcopos. From the establishment of the parish in 1976, Mathai Achen had shepherded the congregation through decades of growth and challenges, from worshipping in temporary locations to finally establishing a permanent home in Bensalem. Following his retirement, Mathai Achen and Kochamma returned to Kerala, where they fulfilled a long-held desire to continue serving through ministry.

On June 1, 2011, Rev. Fr. Shibu Venad Mathai was appointed Vicar of SGMOC, beginning a new chapter of pastoral leadership for the parish.

Growing in Faith, Ministry, and Service

2011–2023

Under the pastoral leadership of Shibu Achen, SGMOC continued to grow in its ministries, facilities, and service to the wider community. In 2014, the parish acquired dedicated burial plots at Rosedale Memorial Park, establishing the SGMOC Cemetery. A monument of our Patron Saint, St. Geevarghese Mar Gregorios of Parumala, was later installed there and dedicated by H.G. Zachariah Mar Nicholovos on September 23, 2018.

Another important milestone came in 2016 when the parish reacquired the property at 4150 Hulmeville Road, which had previously been part of the land acquired during the construction of the church. On August 27, 2016, the property was dedicated as the St. Gregorios Mission and Ministry Center by H.H. Baselios Marthoma Paulose II in the presence of H.G. Zachariah Mar Nicholovos, further expanding the parish's ability to support its ministries and mission.

SGMOC also strengthened its commitment to the surrounding community. On May 7, 2016, the parish held its first SGMOC 5K Run/1 Mile Walk at Neshaminy State Park in Bensalem, with 323 registered participants and proceeds supporting the church's Helping Hands Ministry. The parish continued to expand its spiritual programs with its first Nuhro Retreat, held during the weekend of August 17, 2017. The first of its kind at SGMOC, its success paved the way

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 37 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

for many more retreats in the years that followed. Beginning in 2018, SGMOC also hosted the Unity Prayer Fellowship as part of its involvement with Building a Better Bensalem Together (B3T), bringing together members of the wider community in fellowship and prayer. When the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted normal life in 2020, SGMOC was well prepared to meet the unprecedented challenge. The parish had already established livestreaming services to enable those unable to attend church due to age, illness, or other circumstances to participate in worship from their homes. This existing capability proved invaluable during the pandemic. While many places of worship were forced to suspend or reduce their services, SGMOC continued its regular schedule of worship without interruption, reaching a record number of faithful through online participation. During this difficult period, the parish also continued to support its members and the surrounding community, demonstrating its enduring commitment to faith, fellowship, and service.

In 2023, SGMOC mourned the passing of its founding Vicar, Late Very Rev. K. Mathai Cor Episcopos. From the establishment of the parish in 1976 through decades of challenge, growth, and transformation, Mathai Achen had played a defining role in the journey of SGMOC. His passing marked the loss of a beloved spiritual father whose ministry and legacy remain deeply woven into the history of the parish.

The Pilgrimage Continues

Golden Jubilee and a New Chapter – 2026

The year 2026 became one of the most blessed and memorable years in the history of SGMOC as we celebrated our Golden Jubilee, marking fifty years since the establishment of our parish in 1976. Our Jubilee celebration brought together generations of our parish family along with distinguished guests, including Congressman Brian Fitzpatrick, State Senator Frank Farry, State Representative Kathleen Tomlinson, Bensalem Mayor Joseph DiGirolamo, and other community leaders. During the public meeting, we honored many of our pioneers, senior members, past and present office bearers, and clergy whose faith, sacrifice, and leadership helped shape our parish. The celebration continued with a memorable cultural program presented by our own members and the inauguration of new initiatives, including the Memorial Wall and Vision 2030 and Beyond, looking toward the future of SGMOC.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 38 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Parish History

The Jubilee year also brought an extraordinary blessing to our parish. On August 27, 2026, our Vicar, Rev. Fr. Shibu Venad Mathai, was elected to the episcopate of the Malankara Orthodox Syrian Church by the Malankara Syrian Christian Association. His election was a historic and joyful moment for SGMOC and a special recognition of a life devoted to the ministry of the Church. Shibu Achen is scheduled to be elevated to the monastic rank of Ramban on October 27, 2026, and, God willing, episcopally consecrated on February 4, 2027.

On September 27, 2026, Shibu Achen celebrated his final service at SGMOC as our Vicar, bringing to a close fifteen years of pastoral leadership and marking another significant transition in our history. Rev. Fr. Eby Paulose, who was ordained to the Holy Priesthood at SGMOC in 2016, will assume charge as our new Vicar on October 4, 2026, as SGMOC begins the next chapter of its journey.

As we look back across fifty years—from the first gatherings of Malayalee Christians in Philadelphia, to the establishment of the parish in 1976, through years of struggle, sacrifice, growth, and the building of our spiritual home in Bensalem—we give thanks to God for all those who walked this path before us and all those who continue it today. Our Golden Jubilee is not simply a celebration of where we have been, but a reminder that our pilgrimage of faith continues. May the generations that follow carry forward the same faith, sacrifice, and love for the Church that brought us this far.

“O Lord, You became a refuge to us in generation and generation.” — Psalm 89:1

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 39 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

Our Story

Our community traces its origins to 1962, when Rev. Fr. K. M. Simon celebrated the first Malayalam service in Dr. T. V. Philip's apartment on Pine Street, Philadelphia. After fourteen years of ecumenical Sunday worship, the parish was officially founded in October 1976 by Very Rev. Kaleeckal Mathai Cor Episcopos — first as St. Thomas Indian Orthodox Church, with the Holy Qurbana celebrated at the Church of the Savior Cathedral chapel, 38th & Chestnut Streets.

In 1984, following parish reorganization, our community was reconstituted as St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church — in honor of St. Geevarghese Gregorios of Parumala, the first Indian saint of the Orthodox Church. Rev. Fr. K. Mathai continued as Vicar.

A 1994 attempt to build on Verree Road was prevented by zoning. In 1995 the parish purchased its first permanent home at 7721 Torresdale Avenue, Philadelphia. Land at 4136 Hulmeville Road, Bensalem was acquired in 2005 (with adjacent property added in 2006); the new church was first occupied on Christmas Day 2008 and consecrated May 22–23, 2009.

In 2011, our parish hosted the historic Metropolitan Enthronement of His Grace Zachariah Mar Nicholovos, attended by over one thousand faithful. Rev. Fr. Shibu Venad Mathai was appointed Vicar that same year, continuing to lead our vibrant community.

In Memoriam

Proof copy

Very Rev. Kaleeckal Mathai Cor Episcopos

July 3, 1942 – October 12, 2023

Founding Vicar • St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church

❖

A visionary spiritual leader and devoted shepherd, Very Rev. Kaleeckal Mathai Cor Episcopos played a foundational role in establishing and nurturing the Malankara Orthodox community in Philadelphia. From his early calling to the priesthood, he dedicated his life to the Church, guiding the congregation through its formative years, growth, and the establishment of a permanent home in Bensalem. His unwavering faith, humility, compassion, and tireless dedication continue to inspire all of us.

Ordained as a deacon in 1974 and to the priesthood in 1975, he served as the Founding Vicar of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church from 1976 to 2011. In 1996, he was elevated to Cor Episcopos and also served the Northeast American Diocese as a Diocesan Council Member and Clergy Secretary.

❖

May his blessed memory be eternal.

St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church 54 Golden Jubilee 1976 – 2026

In Memoriam

Proof copy

Rev. Fr. Dr. Paul Varki

February 7, 1931 – March 26, 2014

Pioneer • Spiritual Leader • Faithful Servant

❖

Rev. Fr. Dr. Paul Varki was a pioneering spiritual leader whose dedication helped lay the foundation for Malankara Orthodox worship in the Philadelphia region. Beginning in 1965, he played an instrumental role in bringing Orthodox Christians together for worship, fostering an ecumenical fellowship that eventually contributed to the establishment of the parish in 1976.

After obtaining his Master of Divinity degree from Princeton Theological Seminary, he pursued further studies in psychology, earning his doctorate. His academic accomplishments complemented his spiritual calling, reflecting his lifelong commitment to faith, education, and service.

Through his vision, leadership, and tireless efforts, Rev. Fr. Paul Varki helped nurture the early Orthodox community in Philadelphia. His contributions remain an important part of the history of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church and the spiritual heritage of generations who followed.

❖

May his blessed memory be eternal.

Mariamma Varki and Family

August 17, 1934 – March 26, 2011

Deacon • St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church

❖

Dn. Markose Mani was a devoted servant of God and a faithful deacon of St. Gregorios Malankara Orthodox Church. With a humble heart and unwavering faith, he faithfully served the Church and its community for many years, supporting the growth of the parish through his dedication, love, and quiet leadership.

Known for his gentle spirit, kindness, and deep commitment to the Church, Dn. Markose played an important role in the spiritual and communal life of our parish. His faithful presence, service at the altar, and care for the parish family touched many lives and remain an inspiration to all of us.

We remember him with deep gratitude for his life of service and the lasting legacy he leaves in our hearts.

Our Sunday School

A Legacy of Faith, A Future of Promise

Celebrating fifty years of nurturing faith and building generations

“Train up a child in the way he should go; even when he is old, he will not depart from it.” — Proverbs 22:6

From modest classrooms on Torresdale Avenue to a growing ministry in Bensalem, our Sunday School has continued its mission of forming young hearts in Orthodox faith, worship, fellowship and service. The reflections that follow are shared in the voices of the principals who helped guide this ministry through different seasons of parish life.

Our Sunday School family — students, teachers, clergy and families.

Sunday School Leadership Through the Years
